card.hook: The garden covers 750,000 square metres, so don't even try to fit it into one photo. Pick a spot where the pond, the pines and Mt. Shiun line up, and let the rest go.
card.stand_here: Stand near 栗林公園, about 30 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the pond, pines and mountain together. Go to 0.5x when you're close to a pavilion or a clipped pine, and try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out one pine, a teahouse roof or the koi.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the main subject, then slide it a touch darker if the sky is bright, so the greens and the reflections stay rich.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon gives softer light and fewer people. A calm day gives you the clearest reflections in the water.
card.selfie_here: Head to the Engetsu-kyo (Crescent Moon) Bridge over Nanko (South) Pond. Stand on the arched bridge with the Kikugetsu-tei teahouse and Mt. Shiun behind you, use the front camera at 0.5x and let that classic garden backdrop fill the frame over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the small Hiraiho Hill in the south-west corner of the South Garden while you stand on the crescent bridge, because that's where the postcard shot comes from.
card.rules_and_safety: Ask permission before photographing at teahouses or other special areas. Climbing Hiraiho Peak on a rainy day can be slippery.
card.challenge: Find a koi near the water's edge, shoot a Live Photo, then scroll back and pick the frame where it looks the most dramatic.
card.good_to_know: Work began in 1625 under the local feudal lord Ikoma Takatoshi, and later lords kept improving the garden until it was completed in 1745. It opened to the public in 1875 and was named a Special Place of Scenic Beauty in 1953. It's a major public garden that may have an entry fee and set opening times, so check the official site before you go.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand near 栗林公園, about 30 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east.

selfie_spots.why: From the bridge, the teahouse and the mountain fill the frame, which gives a classic garden backdrop for a selfie.

selfie_spots.why: One guide calls this one of the garden's most iconic compositions, combining the bridge, its reflection and the mountain.

ask_someone_spot.detail: stand on the small hill in the south-west corner; from here the crescent bridge makes the postcard shot, so have the visitor on the bridge. A rest area sits at the foot of the hill near the bridge.

selfie_research.notes: No page names a selfie stick rule for Ritsurin Garden. One guide says to check the garden's tripod rules but does not state them, so no tripod rule is listed. The Engetsu-kyo bridge is described as wooden in one source and as a stone arch in another, so the second spot's naming is uncertain. Rules from the Phoenix garden, Tokyo Disney and Disney World pages were excluded because they do not apply to this garden. The pages give no map coordinates, so the spots are unverified on a map beyond their names.

card.hook: Picture the sun sinking into the Seto Inland Sea while the first lights of Takamatsu blink on below you. Yashima does that in one frame, and it's why guides call it one of Japan's best sunset and night-view spots.
card.stand_here: Stand on the terrace at 獅子の霊厳, on the western edge of the mountain-top plateau. Face west, out over the sea, with the city spread out below you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the sunset and the city below. Go to 0.5x for more coastline and sky, then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out boats on the water.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the brightest part of the sky, then slide it a little darker so the sunset colours don't wash out.
card.best_time: Come in the late afternoon and get settled for the last half hour of daylight. Stay for the time just after sunset, when the sky colours and the first city lights share the same frame.
card.selfie_here: Try the Yukakutei observation deck on the summit. Use the front camera at 0.5x, hold it a little low and let the wide sea-and-island view fill in behind you. For a different mood, the stone path under the ubame oak tunnel makes a lovely green backdrop, and a hat or small prop helps.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand back far enough to fit the whole Yukakutei deck and the wide scenery in the shot, and stand where the sun lights your face.
card.rules_and_safety: The mountain path can be slippery, so a sunny day is best. The terrace is reported as freely accessible, but check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Catch a boat crossing the water with the sunset colours behind it, then shoot the same view again once the city lights are on.
card.good_to_know: Yashima is home to Yashima-ji, the 84th temple on the Shikoku 88 temple pilgrimage. The mountain was also a decisive battleground in the Genpei War (1180–1185) between the Taira and Minamoto clans. If you have time, 遊鶴亭 has a wide view of the sea and islands with boats crossing, and 長崎の鼻 shows boats passing close below a small cape.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the terrace at 獅子の霊厳, on the western edge of the mountain-top plateau. Face west, out over the sea, with the city spread out below you.

selfie_spots.why: The oak branches form a green tunnel over the trail, and a hat or small prop adds to the mood, so the trail itself is the Yashima scenery you stand in.

selfie_research.notes: No page I found says that Yashima itself is directly behind the visitor at either selfie spot; the backdrops are the oak tunnel and the summit sea-and-island view, so the 'landmark behind' test is only loosely met. Kotoden Yashima Station (pastel station building, wear something pink) was left out because it is a station, not the landmark. No page states any selfie stick or tripod rule, so the rules list is empty. The 35-minute walk time is from the photo guide and may vary. The sources are mixed in age (some are about 2 years old) and I did not verify current conditions at the summit.

card.hook: Trains, ferries, buses and taxis all squeeze into this one patch of waterfront, and that's the fun of it. Think of it as a photo of a busy harbour at work, not a single landmark.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, about 380 m north of Sunport Takamatsu, and face south. Take a wide first shot from there, then walk closer for details.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the buildings and their surroundings in one frame. Switch to 1x for a natural view, then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out signs and rooflines.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line up the building edges with them, and hold your phone level at chest height so the buildings don't lean.
card.best_time: Late afternoon into early evening is a good bet, when the light is softer and the building lights start to come on. Midday gives clear, bright views, but expect more people about.
card.selfie_here: Try the Liminal Air -core- artwork by the port at 8 Sunport: use the front camera, zoom 0.5x, and keep the artwork over your shoulder. For an evening shot, walk out to the end of the Tamamo breakwater, where the red glass lighthouse glows at dusk. Check your framing on the spot, as Sunport itself may not fit behind you at either place.
card.rules_and_safety: The district mixes public areas, shops, a hotel and transport facilities, so check the official site for any restrictions inside particular buildings.
card.challenge: Catch one person walking through your frame, mid-stride, heading for a ferry or a train. Then take a second shot after they've gone and see which one you like better.
card.good_to_know: Sunport Takamatsu stands on the site of the former Takamatsu Freight Depot in Hamanochō. Today it holds a shopping mall, a hotel, apartments, convenience stores and several restaurants. It's also the passenger terminal for JR Shikoku's Takamatsu Station and the Port of Takamatsu ferries, and JR Shikoku has its headquarters here.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the phone icon on the map, about 380 m north of Sunport Takamatsu, and face south. Take a wide first shot from there, then walk closer for details.

selfie_spots.name: Liminal Air -core- artwork at Takamatsu Port (8 Sunport)
selfie_spots.detail: at the artwork by the port, at 8 Sunport
selfie_spots.why: A visitor guide lists this port artwork as a recommended photo spot, and its pictures are often used to symbolize the Setouchi Triennale.

selfie_spots.name: Takamatsu Harbor Tamamo Pier Lighthouse (Seto Shirube), end of the breakwater
selfie_spots.detail: on the Tamamo breakwater, out to the end where the red glass lighthouse stands
selfie_spots.why: A guide tells visitors to walk to the end of the breakwater to take photos, and the lighthouse glows red at dusk, which suits evening pictures.

sources.title: Takamatsu Harbor Tamamo Pier Lighthouse (Seto Shirube)

selfie_research.notes: I found no page that places a visitor with Sunport Takamatsu directly behind them, so neither selfie spot is confirmed as a spot with the landmark in the background. Both were picked from pages about the port and lighthouse, and the framing should be checked on site. No page named a spot where a passer-by should stand to photograph a visitor with the whole landmark, so ask_someone_spot is null. No page stated selfie stick or tripod rules, and none gave a safety point for this site. The Liminal Air entry is a sculpture at the port, and its page does not say whether it is a good background for selfies.
